entities.summary:
The Basilica of Sacré-Cœur (Sacred Heart) on Montmartre hill in Paris, consecrated in 1919 after 44 years of construction (begun 1875), is the most politically charged religious building in France — built as a 'national vow' of atonement for the French defeat in the Franco-Prussian War (1870) and the Paris Commune (1871), which conservatives interpreted as divine punishment for France's moral decline. Montmartre hill, where the Paris Commune began (the Commune members shot two generals here in March 1871), became the site of the national Catholic atonement monument — a deliberate political provocation.

The Sacré-Cœur project was promoted by Catholics who saw France's 1870 defeat by Prussia as God's punishment for the liberal anti-clerical politics of the Second Empire. The National Assembly authorized the church's construction in 1873, with the specific political intent of asserting Catholic France against anticlerical republicanism. The site on Montmartre — the birthplace of the Paris Commune — was chosen by conservatives to symbolically 'reclaim' the hill from revolutionary leftism.

The basilica was designed by Paul Abadie in Romano-Byzantine style, with its distinctive white travertine stone that actually becomes whiter with rain (calcite washing). The interior houses the largest mosaic in France — Christ in Majesty (475 m²), designed by Luc-Olivier Merson. The bell (La Savoyarde, 19 tons) is France's largest. Sacré-Cœur receives 10 million visitors annually, making it one of Paris's most visited monuments, though it remains a liturgically active basilica with perpetual adoration since 1885.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sacré-Cœur is the only major cathedral built as an explicit political act — the Catholic right deliberately constructing it on the Paris Commune's birthplace as a statement of atonement and reclamation — making it the most politically charged religious building in France.
